a: It means fixing or replacing a buried sewer line without digging it up from end to end. With lining, a resin-soaked tube is pulled or inverted into the old pipe and cured in place, often from a cleanout with no digging at all. With pipe bursting, a new pipe is pulled through the path of the old one between two small pits. Either way, the lawn, driveway, trees and porch in between usually stay where they are.

q: How do you decide between lining, bursting and digging?
a: We decide from camera footage, not from a guess. Lining suits a pipe that still holds its shape and slope but leaks, cracks or lets roots in. Bursting suits a line that is too broken, too deformed or too small to line. Conventional digging is the answer when the grade itself is wrong or the route has to change. We show you the video and explain why the other options were set aside.

A liner takes the shape of the pipe it cures inside, so it copies the pipe's problems as well as sealing it. Lining is the wrong call when a section has sagged and holds water (a belly), when heaving soil has pushed joints out of line so the path steps up or down, when the pipe has collapsed or flattened, and when the slope is too flat to carry waste. Deformed Orangeburg is a common example. Those lines need bursting or a dig, and we will say so.

q: How long does a trenchless repair take?
a: For a typical house, lining is usually finished in one day once the pipe has been cleaned and inspected; the resin cure itself takes a few hours. Pipe bursting normally takes one to two days because two access pits have to be dug and then backfilled and compacted. A conventional replacement takes longer, depending on depth, length and how much concrete or landscaping sits over the line.

q: Can we use water in the house during the work?
a: Plan on no drains being used while the line is open and the liner or new pipe goes in, which for most homes is a single working day. Sinks, toilets, showers, the washer and the dishwasher all feed the same sewer, so all of them are affected. We tell you before we start when the shutoff begins and when you can run water again, and we check the line on camera before handing it back.

q: Do I need a permit, and who issues it?
a: Usually yes, and in the Denver metro the answer to who issues it depends on the address. The city or town typically handles plumbing permits and any cut into a street, alley or sidewalk, while the sewer main may belong to the city or to a separate sanitation district with its own rules at the tap. We confirm the jurisdiction for your property, pull the permits and schedule the inspections.

q: Do you need access inside the house?
a: Often, yes. Many Front Range homes have their only cleanout in the basement or crawlspace, and lining from inside lets us reach the whole line without touching the yard. If there is an exterior cleanout or a good spot to dig a small access pit, we may not need to come in at all. We cover floors and work areas and tell you ahead of time what we need to reach.

q: Is trenchless always less expensive than digging?
a: Not always, and anyone who promises that without seeing the line is guessing. Trenchless often costs less overall on long runs or when the pipe passes under a driveway, porch, mature trees or a street, because those do not have to be torn out and rebuilt. On a short, shallow run across open lawn, a conventional dig can be competitive. Our estimates are free, and we give you the scope in writing.

q: Why do sewer estimates differ so much?
a: Mostly because contractors are pricing different jobs. One quote may cover a spot repair while another covers the full line, out to and including the tap. One may assume lining a pipe that has a belly, which will not solve the problem. Others leave out permits, street-cut work, cleaning or a final camera run. Ask each company to show you the footage and to put in writing what length of pipe it is fixing and how.

q: Will homeowners insurance pay for a failing sewer line?
a: Usually it is worth checking, but do not count on it. Standard policies commonly exclude damage from wear, age and deterioration, which covers most cracked, root-filled or sagging laterals. Coverage for water that backs up into the house is often a separate add-on rather than part of the base policy. Service-line endorsements do exist on some policies. Check your policy, or call your agent, before the work starts so you know where you stand.

q: Who owns the sewer line under the street in the Denver area?
a: In most Front Range cities and sanitation districts, the property owner owns the whole service line from the house to the public main, and often the connection at the main as well, even where the pipe runs under the street or an alley. Arvada, Brighton and St. Vrain Sanitation District, for example, put the connection on the owner. Rules do vary, so confirm with your city or sanitation district which part is yours.

q: What is a special sanitation district, and does it matter?
a: Much of the suburban and unincorporated metro gets sewer service from a special district rather than the city whose name is on the mailing address. Lakewood, for instance, runs sewer only for part of the north side; other providers serve the rest. The district that owns the main can set its own requirements for work at the tap, inspections and contractor approval. Your sewer bill usually names the provider.

q: How does expansive soil affect sewer lines here?
a: Much of the Front Range sits on clay that swells when it gets wet and shrinks when it dries. That movement can lift or drop sections of a buried line, pulling joints apart, cracking pipe and leaving low spots where waste settles. The Colorado Geological Survey calls swelling soil one of the state's most damaging geologic hazards. A camera shows whether the line has only cracked, which lining can fix, or has lost its grade.

q: My house was built in the 1950s or 1960s. Could the sewer be Orangeburg?
a: It could. Orangeburg is a fiber pipe made of wood pulp soaked in coal-tar pitch, and it was widely used in postwar housing until production ended in the 1970s. Over time it softens and flattens into an oval, blisters on the inside and lets roots in. Many Front Range homes of that era have clay tile instead, and some have a mix of both. Only a camera inspection will tell you which you have.

q: Can you do sewer work in a Colorado winter?
a: Yes. Lining is done from inside the pipe and the resin cure is controlled, so cold weather rarely stops it, although we take extra care with water and equipment when it is below freezing. Frozen ground makes digging access pits or trenches slower, which can affect bursting and conventional replacement. A backed-up sewer does not wait for spring, and we work year-round, open 24 hours a day, seven days a week.

q: Should I get a sewer scope before buying a house?
a: We recommend it for almost any resale home, and especially for houses built before the 1980s. A general home inspection normally stops at the foundation wall, but the lateral out to the main is typically the buyer's responsibility after closing. A camera run can find roots, Orangeburg, cracked clay, offsets from soil movement or a belly while you still have time to ask questions. Ask for the recording, not just a summary.

q: How long have you been doing trenchless work?
a: All Sewer and Plumbing Services has done trenchless sewer work in Colorado since 2009. Owner Jeff Haug trained on and bought Perma-Liner lining equipment at a time when almost nobody in the state offered lining. The company used to operate as Sewer Solutions and is based in Westminster, with dedicated trenchless trucks and crews serving homes, businesses and public agencies across the Front Range.
